P1.evidence: Setter read-back was done properly and named: 'you spoke with Kim two days ago, something like that. So he briefed me in on where you're at right now, but I'm kind of an old-school guy. I would love to hear it from you, too.' The open question followed immediately and cleanly: 'what is it that you're trying to fix right now in terms of fitness and how we can support you with that?' The frame itself was two parts of four — where you are and how we can help — with nothing about what is in the way or what he needs, and no agreement was requested.

P2.evidence: Strong. Age was asked directly ('mind me asking, how old are you?'), though height and weight never were, on a call whose stated goal is visible abs. Work was asked with genuine curiosity and produced the whole shift pattern: 'What do you do for a living that you have to get up at four and be in the office at five?' followed by finish time and gym timing. The injury sequence was the best-run in the batch — 'What kind of injuries?', then 'apart from the injuries, do you feel in your body any limitations in your movements, any stiffness?', then, crucially, 'Did you [have] an x-ray or, I don't know, some kind of a test done?' Diet was taken in layers: daily pattern, an example meal plan, then snacks specifically, then the guilty pleasure. Sleep and energy were both asked and cross-checked against the 4am alarm. The gap is P2c: no health-conditions question at all, so the only medical information on the call is what the injury probe happened to surface.

P3.evidence: The first half ran and the second half did not exist. 'Is there anything specific that you want to achieve in terms of your physique?' produced the abs, and the rep did the right thing by probing rather than accepting it: 'Why are abs so important to you?' He also asked P3c almost verbatim — 'Do you feel that right now there's something left on the table because of the injuries, that you're not in the shape to actually do some activities?' — and got a flat 'No, I don't think so', which is the moment the phase needed rescuing and did not get it. Nothing was asked about what moving better would do for him, nothing about who else this impacts, nothing driven through to identity or longevity, and no reflect-back. The deepest material obtained on a sixty-minute call was 'I looked good when I had them' and 'I felt more confident.' The rep supplied the emotional content himself, twice, with borrowed stories about his own hips and about a 55-year-old CEO, rather than extracting it.

P4.evidence: Well run. 'Why did you quit in the first place?' was asked directly and produced a detailed account of the injure-rest-reinjure loop, including the two-week and one-month waiting periods and the re-flare within days. The rep pushed on the anomaly rather than accepting it — 'still, it's weird that those injuries occur. Did you [have] an x-ray or some kind of a test done?' — which got the prospect to name his own root cause in his own words: 'I'm thinking it's something in my technique, or maybe how I'm lifting is the root cause.' That is the ideal setup for the video form-check pillar and the rep did later connect the two. Only the explicit one-thing-in-the-way question and the information-isn't-the-problem line were not run.

P5.evidence: Not run at all. No two-year question, no willing-to-settle, no why-not, no line in the sand. The material was unusually available: a man who has just realised on the call that he has not trained in three years — 'That's bad now that I think about that' — who now sits down for ten hours a day and said 'Oh no, that's not good, because then I'm just gonna put on weight.' Every ingredient of a consequence frame was volunteered and none of it was used. When the price landed there was no cost of inaction on the table to weigh it against, only a wish to look good.

P6.evidence: Both questions asked, in the right order and before anything was presented. The commitment question came first, framed honestly: 'it's going to suck. Especially in the beginning... are you willing to show up and are you going to be committed to actually doing the work?' — answered 'Yeah. Oh, yeah, definitely. I actually am, dude.' The belief question was then asked after the pillars and before the price: 'if you had the right training, nutrition, and accountability, do you feel that you would get to your goals and that would be the way for your future?' / 'I do, actually. Yeah, I really do.' He then re-confirmed commitment one more time immediately before naming the number. Clean execution of the phase.

P11.evidence: Payment was worked hard for over twenty minutes — four structures, a live escalation to an owner, two financing applications on two devices, one link re-sent by email — and nothing was collected. The Trevor onboarding call was named as the destination at 00:37:47 and never scheduled. The agreement, welcome email, Skool link and questionnaire were not mentioned at any point. No follow-up time was booked before the recording ends, which is the most damaging omission: a prospect this warm was left with a declined credit application and no next step on tape.

objection_plays.detail: Most of the financial picture was taken and the sequencing around it was wrong. He got monthly surplus ('roughly how much do you have left in your account?' / about $300), credit cards and the limit ('Do you use credit cards?' / one, $300 limit), and savings ('is it like five figure, four figure?'). He did not isolate before opening the conversation, did not run the SHOULD I versus HOW reframe, and did not ask about investments. The bigger problem is what he did with the answers: $300 a month of surplus against a $300 credit limit is a complete answer, and rather than treating it as a disqualification he escalated to an owner by text and walked the prospect down a ladder — $6,000, then 50/50, then $1,200 a month, then a lender, then $4,000, then the lender again. Two of those quotes are problems in themselves: $1,200 a month over six months is $7,200, and the $4,000 three-month tier is not a product. Compare the Hariharan call the same day, where the same open wallet found real capacity and the price never moved.

Clinical fit, and the sharpest instance in the corpus because the rep got all the way to the right question and then did nothing with the answer. He asked 'Did you [have] an x-ray or some kind of a test done?' and heard 'No, I never did.' A recurring shoulder and neck problem across two years, never assessed, in a man about to start overhead ballistic loading, and the script has no move that turns that answer into a clearance requirement. The rep's substitute was the form-check mechanic. Adding one line to Phase 2 — 'has anyone ever looked at it, and did they tell you what to avoid?' — would convert an existing question into a screen.

Third-party credit declined live, twice, which nothing in the playbook contemplates. 'We're sorry we're unable to offer a payment plan at this time' is an external solvency verdict delivered in front of both parties, and the scripted response set has no move for it. The rep treated it as a technical fault — retried on a laptop, re-sent by email, then re-applied at a lower amount — which turned a clean stopping point into twelve more minutes of descending offers. A rule is needed: a declined application ends the money conversation and routes to the lower-priced product.

Prospect below the price floor with an in-house product that fits, and no scripted route to it. Primal University at $199 a month, cancel anytime, was offered by this same rep to a prospect with a €200 monthly ceiling the previous day. This prospect stated a $300 monthly surplus and was never told the product exists. There is no step in the playbook that says what to do when the financial picture comes back under the threshold, so the rep discounted the flagship instead of downselling.

notes: Phases 2, 4 and 6 were run properly and Phases 3 and 5 collapsed, so the rep reached the price with a fully mapped body and no emotional stake — 'I want my abs back' is not enough weight to carry $6,000. The specific coaching point is the money ladder: a $300 monthly surplus against a $300 credit limit is a finished answer, and the correct next move was Primal University at $199, not four descending structures and two declined credit applications. Fix the six-month instalment quote as well; $1,200 a month is $7,200.
